When Everyday Stress Stops Feeling Manageable

Stress is a normal part of adult life, especially when you are juggling work, family, money, and relationships. But there can be a point where what used to feel manageable starts to feel heavy, constant, and confusing. You might notice yourself feeling tired all the time, snapping at people you care about, or lying awake at night with your mind racing.

Around autumn in Brisbane, many adults feel this strain more sharply. The daylight hours feel shorter, work tends to ramp up, school demands build, and the cooler evenings can make it tempting to just collapse on the couch and zone out. It can be hard to tell if you are just stressed, burning out, or living with anxiety.

Understanding the difference between burnout and anxiety can help you choose the right kind of support. For many people, that includes adult therapy services that provide a safe place to work out what is really going on and what to do next.

Burnout Basics: When Long-Term Stress Drains You Dry

Burnout is not just having a bad week. It is a state of physical, emotional, and mental exhaustion that builds over time when stress goes on without enough rest or support. It often shows up around work, caregiving, or study, where you feel like expectations keep growing and you cannot step away.

Common signs of burnout include:

  • Feeling tired most of the time, even after sleep
  • Feeling emotionally flat, numb, or detached
  • Growing cynical about work, family roles, or responsibilities
  • Struggling to care about things you used to value
  • Finding it harder to focus, finish tasks, or make decisions

Many adults notice burnout creeping in around the middle of the year. There may be performance reviews at work, school assessments, or financial pressure as the end of the financial year gets closer. You might tell yourself to just push through for “a few more weeks”, then realise that months have passed and nothing has changed.

Burnout often feels like you have nothing left to give. Instead of feeling worried or nervous, you might feel empty, stuck, or disconnected from your own life.

Anxiety Signs: When Your Mind Will Not Switch Off

Anxiety is different. It is more about ongoing worry, fear, or dread that does not match what is actually happening around you. With anxiety, you may feel on high alert much of the time, even during small tasks or quiet moments.

Signs of anxiety can include:

  • Racing thoughts or constant “what if” questions
  • Trouble falling asleep or staying asleep
  • Physical tension, like a tight chest, sore neck, shaky hands, or a churning stomach
  • Restlessness, fidgeting, or feeling unable to relax
  • Feeling easily irritated or snappy with loved ones

Anxiety often shows up around everyday triggers, such as:

  • Worrying about how you are performing at work
  • Getting stuck in fears about your child’s learning or behaviour
  • Feeling scared about relationship conflict or breakups
  • Turning news about global events or money problems into worst-case scenarios

Even if the day is not especially stressful, your mind might keep replaying past events or predicting future disasters. You can feel exhausted and wired at the same time.

Burnout vs Anxiety: How to Tell Them Apart

Burnout and anxiety can feel quite different on the inside, even though they can overlap.

Emotionally, burnout often feels:

  • Flat or empty
  • Disconnected from work or people
  • Low in motivation, even for things you usually like

Anxiety often feels:

  • Wired or on edge
  • Full of “what if” thoughts
  • Like your mind is always scanning for danger

Their patterns can differ, too. Burnout usually links to a specific area of ongoing overload, such as your job, caring for a family member, parenting, or intense study. You might notice that when you are away from that role, you feel a little better, but going back into it feels unbearable.

Anxiety is more likely to spread across many parts of life. It might show up at work, at home, at the shops, when you are trying to sleep, or when you think about the future. It can be harder to find an “off switch” because the worry keeps shifting topics.

It is also common for burnout and anxiety to feed into each other. Long-term burnout can lead to anxious thoughts like “I am never going to catch up”, and long-term anxiety can wear you down until you reach burnout. Adult therapy services can help tease apart what is happening for you and give you tools for both.

When It Is Time to Seek Therapy Support

Stress, burnout, and anxiety sit on a spectrum, so it can be hard to know when to seek help. Some practical red flags include:

  • Symptoms that last for more than a few weeks without easing
  • Avoiding friends, family, or the hobbies you usually enjoy
  • Struggling to keep up with work, parenting, or study
  • More arguments and tension in your close relationships
  • Using alcohol, food, or other substances more often just to get through the day

There are emotional warning signs too:

  • Feeling stuck, trapped, or like life is on repeat
  • Telling yourself “I just have to survive this phase” month after month
  • Feeling guilty or like a failure for not coping “better”

You do not need to wait for a crisis before seeking support. Therapy can be helpful at the first sign that your usual coping tools are not working as well as they used to, especially around the mid-year period when many adults feel extra pressure.

How Adult Therapy Services Can Help You Recover

Seeing a clinical psychologist for burnout or anxiety usually starts with a conversation about what your life looks like right now. Together, you can explore your symptoms, daily routines, stressors, and strengths. The aim is to build a clear picture of what you are facing and what might help.

Adult therapy services may include:

  • Cognitive Behaviour Therapy, which helps you notice and gently change unhelpful thought patterns
  • Acceptance and mindfulness-based strategies, which help you relate differently to stress and worry
  • Practical stress management and problem-solving skills, tailored to your situation

At Michelle Barratt Psychology, we offer adult support in Toowong, Wynnum West, and through Telehealth, which can be a good fit if you are working, caring for others, or based in another part of Brisbane or Queensland. Having flexible options can make it easier to fit regular sessions around your week and keep momentum with your goals.

Over time, therapy can help you rebuild energy, set healthier boundaries, and respond differently to stress and anxiety. It is not about “fixing” you, but about giving you space, tools, and support so life feels a little lighter and more manageable.

Small First Steps to Protect Your Well-being Now

While professional support is often the most helpful way to change deeper patterns, there are also gentle steps you can start to take now to care for yourself.

You might like to try:

  • Setting one small boundary at work, such as a clear finish time a few days a week
  • Spending a little time outdoors in daylight, even for a short walk or coffee break
  • Turning off screens a bit earlier at night and giving yourself a calmer wind-down
  • Planning one small enjoyable activity each week, even if it is only for 20 minutes

It can also help to check in with yourself regularly. Once a week, pause and ask, “How am I really coping?” Notice any shifts in:

  • Sleep patterns or energy levels
  • Mood or patience with others
  • Motivation or interest in daily life

If you notice that burnout or anxiety signs are hanging around or getting worse, adult therapy services can offer structured support to help you recover.
